cases.candidate_question: Is the derivative of the ith coordinate projection the value xᵢ at the point?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. Even at x=0, the ith projection has derivative h↦hᵢ, which is nonzero when i exists, while the proposed scalar value is zero. The derivative is a functional, not a scalar point value.

cases.candidate_question: Does varying one coordinate have velocity equal to the base vector x?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The velocity is eᵢ independently of x. At the zero base vector it is still eᵢ≠0. A valid index ensures the selected coordinate exists.

cases.candidate_question: For a coordinate slice t↦f(update(x,i,t)), can its derivative at t=0 always be substituted for the partial derivative at x?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The slice returns x at t=xᵢ. For f(t)=t² on ℝ and base coordinate x=3, the slice derivative at the intended point is 6; at t=0 it is 0.

cases.candidate_question: Do existing input-coordinate partial derivatives alone imply a total derivative?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The axis-jump family in mv_v5_partials_without_continuity has both block derivatives zero at the origin and is not even continuous there. Component assembly requires full Fréchet derivatives of output components.

cases.candidate_question: Is differentiability of just one output component enough?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The map t↦(|t|,t) has a differentiable second component but is not differentiable at zero because its first component is not.

cases.candidate_question: May the input and output indices be reversed in the Jacobian without transposition?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. For f(t)=(t,t²), the Jacobian has 2 output rows and 1 input column. Reversing the roles gives a matrix of the wrong shape.

cases.candidate_question: May the Jacobian factors in the chain rule be reversed?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. Take linear maps with A=[[1,1],[0,1]] and B=[[2,0],[0,1]]. For g∘f the product BA=[[2,2],[0,1]], whereas AB=[[2,1],[0,1]].

cases.candidate_question: Does differentiability alone imply that the first-order remainder is bounded by C‖h‖² near zero?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. f(t)=|t|^(3/2) is differentiable with derivative zero at zero, but its remainder divided by t² is |t|^(-1/2), unbounded as t tends to zero.

cases.candidate_question: Can the neighborhood partial derivatives and their joint continuity be replaced by two partial derivatives existing just at the point?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The nonzero-amplitude axis-jump family has zero block partial derivatives at the origin and is discontinuous there. Isolated partials do not satisfy the joint-continuity criterion.

cases.candidate_question: Does a C^k function always have a C^k derivative field, with no lost derivative?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. f(t)=t|t| is C¹ with derivative 2|t|, but that derivative is not differentiable at zero. The theorem requires C^(k+1) to obtain a C^k derivative field.

cases.candidate_question: For arbitrary bilinear B, can the derivative of B(x,x) be written 2B(x,h)?
cases.mathematical_reason: Only with symmetry. For B(u,v)=u₁v₂, x=(0,1), h=(1,0), the actual derivative B(x,h)+B(h,x)=1, whereas 2B(x,h)=0.

cases.candidate_question: Is the Hessian of x↦B(x,x) equal to B, without its transpose term?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. For B(u,v)=u₁v₂ the Hessian is B+B.flip. Evaluated at u=(0,1),v=(1,0) it is 1, while B(u,v)=0.

cases.candidate_question: Can the quadratic term B(h,h) be removed from the exact expansion?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. On ℝ take B(u,v)=uv, x=0 and h=1. The value at x+h is 1, while the constant and first-order terms at x are both zero.

cases.candidate_question: Does the weak Lagrange theorem imply that the objective multiplier b is nonzero?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. With constraint f(t)=t², objective g(t)=t and x=0, the level set is {0} and hence g has a constrained extremum. A=0 and B=1, so aA+bB=0 forces b=0.

cases.candidate_question: Can B=λA be concluded when the constraint derivative may vanish?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The strictly differentiable constraint f(t)=t² and objective g(t)=t have a constrained extremum at zero, but A=0 and B=1. No scalar multiple of A equals B.

cases.candidate_question: Must the constraint multiplier vector itself be nonzero?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. For the single regular constraint f(t)=t and constant objective g(t)=0 at zero, the multiplier identity forces the constraint multiplier to be zero; the objective multiplier can be nonzero. Only their combined vector is required to be nonzero.

cases.candidate_question: May Fubini be applied merely because both signed iterated integrals are finite?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. On (0,1)² let f(x,y)=(x²−y²)/(x²+y²)², extended by zero elsewhere. Integrating y first gives π/4, and x first gives −π/4. Its absolute product integral diverges near the origin, so it is not product integrable.

cases.candidate_question: Can any real two-variable function have its integration order exchanged?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. For f(x,y)=(x²−y²)/(x²+y²)² on (0,1)² and zero outside, the two signed iterated integrals are π/4 and −π/4. The missing hypothesis is product integrability.

cases.candidate_question: Does formal separated-product factorization alone certify that the multiple integral exists as an integrable function?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. Take both factors identically 1 on ℝ. Their product is not integrable on ℝ². Lean totalizes these nonintegrable Bochner integrals to zero, so a numerical identity involving totalized integrals is not an existence proof.

cases.candidate_question: Is measurability of the two factors sufficient for product integrability?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. Constant factors f=g=1 on ℝ are measurable, but their product has infinite absolute integral on ℝ².

cases.candidate_question: For a non-Cartesian region may one integrate over its two coordinate projections independently?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The triangle 0<x<1, 0<y<x has area 1/2, whereas the product of its projections is the unit square with area 1. A domain s×t is required for fixed independent section bounds.

cases.candidate_question: Does product integrability imply that every section is integrable?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. Let f(x,y)=1 when x=0 and 0 otherwise on ℝ². It is zero almost everywhere and product integrable, but its x=0 section is the constant 1 on ℝ and is not integrable.

cases.candidate_question: Is the inner-integral function always integrable if each inner integral is finite?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. Set f(x,y)=1_(0,1)(y), independent of x. Every inner integral is 1, but the resulting constant 1 on ℝ is not integrable.

cases.candidate_question: Can the inner integral of |f| be replaced by the absolute value of the signed inner integral?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. The signed sections of (x²−y²)/(x²+y²)² on (0,1)² integrate to 1/(1+x²), an integrable outer function, although the absolute product integral diverges near zero. Cancellation destroys the needed norm control.

cases.candidate_question: In dimension zero should the separated-product integral be zero because there are no factors?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. ℝ⁰ is a singleton with product volume 1, and the empty product is 1. The integral and the empty product of factor integrals are both 1.

cases.candidate_question: For a finite separated product, may one omit the integrability requirement on one factor just because the other factors are integrable?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. In dimension two take f₁=1 on ℝ and f₂=1_(0,1). The second factor is integrable but the product has infinite absolute integral over ℝ². Every factor hypothesis in this sufficient criterion must be supplied.

cases.candidate_question: Can the absolute determinant in volume substitution be replaced by the signed determinant?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. For f(t)=−t on [0,1] and g=1, the image interval [−1,0] has integral 1, whereas the signed-determinant integrand is −1 and gives −1.

cases.candidate_question: Does the change-of-variables integrability equivalence hold without injectivity on the domain?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. On s=ℝ take f(t)=sin t and g=1. The image is [−1,1], where g is integrable, but the weighted pullback |cos t| is not integrable on ℝ. Repeated covering creates infinite multiplicity.

cases.candidate_question: Does injectivity alone guarantee that the image of every measurable set is measurable?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. A bijection from [0,1] onto a nonmeasurable Vitali subset of [0,1] gives an injective restriction with nonmeasurable image. Such a bijection exists since both sets have continuum cardinality. It has no asserted differentiability or measurability.

cases.candidate_question: May an arbitrary supplied vector u(t) be used as the velocity in the potential integral?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. In dimension one take f(x)=x, D=1, c(t)=t on [0,1], but supply u(t)=0. The integral is 0 and the endpoint potential difference is 1; the required curve derivative premise fails.

cases.candidate_question: Does every continuous one-form have path-independent integrals?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. On ℝ² the form D(x,y)(u,v)=−yu+xv integrates to 2π along the unit circle traversed once and to 0 along the constant path at (1,0), with the same endpoints. It is not the derivative of a global scalar potential.

cases.candidate_question: Is the axis-jump family still a discontinuity counterexample when its amplitude a=0?
cases.mathematical_reason: No. For a=0 both branches vanish, so the entire function is identically zero and continuous. The nonzero amplitude assumption is essential.
